claims.claim: The giant was found at Cardiff, New York, on October 16, 1869.
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: There was no genuine need for a well at the spot where the giant was found.
claims.quote: there was no reason why the farmer should dig a well in the spot where the figure was found; that it was convenient neither to the house nor to the barn; that there was already a good spring and a stream of water running conveniently to both

claims.claim: The giant image is from Bain News Service, 1910, public domain.
claims.quote:
Date: 1910
Author: Bain News Service, publisher
Licence: Public domain

claims.claim: The figure measured ten feet four and a half inches.
claims.quote: The length of the giant was 10 feet 4+1⁄2 inches (3.162 m)

claims.claim: A print titled "The Onondaga Giant" showed views of the right and left sides, as he appears lying in state.
claims.quote: THE ONONDAGA GIANT. ... Views of right and left sides, as he appears lying in state.

claims.claim: George Hull was a New York tobacconist and had the figure made in his own form.
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: The giant was designed to imitate Hull's own form.
claims.quote: The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: The stone came from a gypsum quarry in Iowa.
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: In 1868 Hull hired men to quarry a block of gypsum at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling them it was for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York.
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York.

claims.claim: The stereocard image is a View in Cardiff Glen, Iowa, dated 1873, scanned by NYPL.
claims.quote:
View in Cardiff Glen, near Fort Dodge, Iowa.
Date: 1873
Author: Scan by NYPL

claims.claim: The reverse of the stereocard states the block was taken to Chicago, the giant carved, then shipped to New York and buried in a barn lot.
claims.quote: The block was taken to Chicago, the "Giant" carved, and then shipped to the point in New York which gave it its name, where it was buried in a barn lot, and subsequently "discovered".

claims.claim: The card names the perpetrators of the imposture as George Hull and H. B. Martin.
claims.quote: The perpetrators of the imposture are well remembered by old residents of Fort Dodge. Their names were George Hull and H. B. Martin.

claims.claim: Hull removed the hair and beard after a geologist told him hair does not petrify.
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh noted that soluble gypsum buried for centuries in wet earth would not keep fresh tool marks, and called it "a most decided humbug".
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue, pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did), and termed it "a most decided humbug".

claims.claim: Hull confessed to the press on December 10, 1869.
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: On February 2, 1870, both Hull's giant and Barnum's copy were declared fakes in court.
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: It remains unclear whether the Chicago stonecutter who received the block knew what it was for.
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions, it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving

claims.claim: The man who made the giant wanted the hoax to be exposed.
claims.quote: Hull proclaimed that he did not confess because of the pressing criticism, but confessed proudly that he intended for the hoax to be exposed

claims.claim: Hull lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4 and the giants it says once lived on Earth.
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: The revival-meeting argument took place in 1868.
Hull was angered by the credulity around him and set out to show how easily people could be fooled.
claims.quote: Angered by his defeat and the credulity of people, Hull wanted to prove how easily he could fool people with a fake giant.

claims.claim: In Chicago two sculptors carved the block.
claims.quote: Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant.

claims.claim: Sand and water, sulphuric acid, and steel knitting needles in a board were used to age the surface.
claims.quote: Hull first wiped the giant using a sponge soaked with sand and water. The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores. The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: The hoax cost $2,600.
claims.quote: By then, he had spent US$2,600 (equivalent to $63,000 in 2025) for the hoax.

claims.claim: The figure was buried on his cousin William Newell's farm in late November 1868.
claims.quote: On a night in late November 1868, the giant was buried in a hole in Newell's farm.

claims.claim: It was "found" on October 16, 1869, by two men hired to dig a well.
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant.

claims.claim: Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing.
claims.quote: a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant

claims.claim: Three to five hundred people came a day.
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day

claims.claim: Andrew D. White was Cornell's first president and pointed out there was no reason to dig a well in that spot.
claims.quote: Andrew D. White, the first president of Cornell University, made a close inspection of the Cardiff Giant. He noticed that there was no good reason to try to dig a well in the exact spot the giant had been found.

claims.claim: Barnum's copy was made of plaster.
claims.quote: he hired a man to model the giant's shape covertly in wax and create a plaster copy

claims.claim: The Chicago stonecutter was named Edward Burkhardt.
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.

claims.claim: A Michigan arcade displaying a copy says theirs is Barnum's.
claims.quote: The owner of Marvin's Marvelous Mechanical Museum, a coin-operated game arcade and museum of oddities in Farmington Hills, Michigan, has said that the copy displayed there is Barnum's.

claims.claim: The "Onondaga Giant" lithograph is from Popular Graphic Arts.
claims.quote: Author: Popular Graphic Arts
